statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; second-hand, without appraisal), medicines tried for sleep problems in people stopping or cutting down alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioids had mixed results, and better sleep did not reliably mean less drug use. For alcohol, gabapentin gave largely positive results in studies; quetiapine improved waking at night and insomnia in one placebo-controlled trial, with mixed effects on drinking; and trazodone improved sleep measures but in a large placebo-controlled trial was linked with less abstinence during treatment and more drinking after it. For cannabis withdrawal, zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved some sleep measures, but none clearly reduced relapse. For cocaine, modafinil normalized deep sleep in one study from the senior author's laboratory. For opioids, trazodone did not improve sleep in methadone maintenance, and amitriptyline and lorazepam did not differ for withdrawal insomnia in 27 people. Benzodiazepines are often avoided with alcohol because of dependence and overdose risk. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: A review of sleep research says that sleep medicines given to people stopping alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioids sometimes improved sleep, but that did not reliably help them stay off the drug. In one large trial, people stopping alcohol who took trazodone slept better but drank more. These are second-hand findings from a review that did not check study quality.
population: People with alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioid use disorders in early abstinence or treatment, in trials cited by a narrative review
exposure: Medicines for sleep (gabapentin, quetiapine, trazodone, zolpidem, mirtazapine, modafinil, amitriptyline and others)
comparator: Placebo or another medicine, as in the cited trials
outcome: Sleep measures and relapse or drug use
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized; no effect sizes given. Trazodone in alcohol use disorder: better sleep quality but less abstinence during treatment and more drinking after it in a large placebo-controlled trial; amitriptyline against lorazepam in 27 people with opioid-withdrawal insomnia: no difference on most measures.

evidence.locator: Alcohol › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As summarized: gabapentin studied with largely but not entirely positive results; ramelteon and agomelatine only in case series; quetiapine improved wake after sleep onset and subjective insomnia in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, with mixed effects on abstinence and re-hospitalization; trazodone benefited sleep measures but in a large placebo-controlled trial was associated with less abstinence during treatment and increased drinking after it; benzodiazepines are often avoided because of addictive potential and overdose risk with alcohol.

evidence.locator: Cannabis › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As summarized: lofexidine plus oral THC gave the greatest benefit in one study, oral THC alone none; nabilone may reverse withdrawal-related sleep disruption; valproic acid gave no benefit and even some worsening of symptoms, and lithium, nefazodone and bupropion showed no definite benefit; zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved sleep parameters but none conclusively reduced relapse.

evidence.locator: Cocaine › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As summarized: few studies of sleep medicines in people who use cocaine; lisuride changed REM without other benefit; tiagabine increased slow-wave sleep with unnatural architecture and no consistent cognitive benefit; modafinil normalized slow-wave sleep in people who used cocaine chronically, in one study by the senior author's group, with mixed effects on clinical outcome in other trials.

As summarized: methadone and electrostimulation were not effective for insomnia in opioid withdrawal; trazodone did not improve subjective or objective sleep in methadone-maintained patients; amitriptyline and lorazepam did not differ on most sleep measures in a randomized double-blind study of 27 people with opioid-withdrawal insomnia.

risk_of_bias.note: Trials not appraisable through a narrative review.

grade.reasoning: The cited medicine studies are mostly randomized (start high), but seen only through a narrative review, mixed, and unquantified: rated down four levels to very low. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither benefit nor its absence can be shown for any medicine from this source. Stays draft. Status mixed.
